o: My God, from the morning I seek You. My soul thirsts for You, and as I begin this day I want to acknowledge that Your love is better than life itself. Thank You for the night's rest, for the air I breathe and for the chance to rise once again with hope. Everything I have is a gift from You.

Lord, teach me to recognize what is truly of value. So often I run after things that shine but do not last, and I neglect what is eternal. Today I want to put Your kingdom first, seek Your will and live with a heart that prefers You above all things. May my greatest joy be to know You and to walk at Your side.

I pray that You bless my work, my home and my conversations. Give me wisdom to decide well, humility to listen and patience in dealing with people. Keep my loved ones from all harm and accompany those going through difficult times today. May my lips praise You and my hands serve with love. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: Jesus taught the people in parables, and some were very brief but held an immense message. One of them speaks of a merchant who was seeking fine pearls. He was a man who knew his trade, who could tell an ordinary stone from a true jewel, and who devoted his life to finding the best.

One day, as he searched, he found a pearl of great price. It was not just any pearl; it was so precious that he understood at once that no other could compare with it. And then he did something that would surprise anyone: he went and sold everything he had, and bought it.

Before telling this story, Jesus had told another very similar one: that of a man who finds a treasure hidden in a field. Full of joy, he goes and sells all that he has to buy that field. In both accounts there is something in common: the discovery produces joy, and that joy makes everything else seem small. No one forces the merchant or the man in the field; they give everything because they have seen something worth more.

So is the kingdom of heaven, says Jesus. It is not a burden accepted reluctantly, but a treasure discovered with joy. Whoever finds it understands that following Christ is not losing, but gaining what is greatest. That is why the parable invites us today to ask ourselves what we value most and whether we are willing to put God first in our hearts.
m.c: Today, may you walk with the certainty that you already possess what is most precious: the love of God that never ends. Go out with calm, with quiet joy and a heart firm in him. May every step of this day be covered by his faithful care.
m: The parable of the pearl of great price helps us order our priorities. We are all seeking something: security, affection, rest, a good future. And it is not wrong to desire good things. But Jesus teaches us that there is a treasure so great that, when we discover it, everything else falls into its proper place. That treasure is the kingdom of God, that is, living under his love and guidance.

The psalmist expresses it in beautiful words: “Your steadfast love is better than life.” Notice that David wrote this in the wilderness, without comfort, and yet he said his soul was satisfied in God. This reminds us that true wealth does not depend on what we have around us, but on the relationship we have with the Lord.

How can you apply it today? First, devote the first minutes of the morning to being with God, even if they are few. Give thanks, read a verse and ask him to order your day. Second, before making decisions, ask yourself whether this choice brings you closer to or takes you further from what really matters. Third, if today you must choose between two things, choose the one that preserves your peace and your integrity, even if it seems less attractive.

The merchant did not sell everything with sadness, but with resolute joy. When we value God above all, letting go of what holds us back stops being a bitter sacrifice and becomes freedom. Today you can let go of a complaint, a grudge or a useless worry, and take instead the certainty that you possess a pearl no one can take from you. Walk with this wealth in your heart.

o: Good Father, I come to the end of this day with gratitude in my heart. Thank You for sustaining me at every hour, for the strength You gave me when I felt weak and for the people who accompanied me. I acknowledge that not everything went as I wanted, but I know that You were with me and that You never let go of me.

Jesus, You know what it is to feel anguish. In the garden of Gethsemane, You prayed with a soul full of sorrow and entrusted Yourself to the Father's will. Today I want to do the same with my burdens. I give You my fears, my weariness and everything I cannot change. I pray that You do Your will in my life, for Your ways are higher than mine.

Give me deep rest tonight. Calm my mind, quiet my thoughts and fill my house with Your peace. Take care of those who are alone, of the sick and of those who suffer in silence. When I wake, may I feel Your comfort and have courage to begin again. Thank You, because with You I am not alone. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: After celebrating the Passover meal with his disciples, Jesus went out with them to a place called Gethsemane, at the foot of the Mount of Olives. It was night and the atmosphere was heavy with tension. Jesus knew what was approaching, and that night, he wanted to be in prayer.

He told his disciples to sit down while he prayed. He took with him Peter, James and John, and began to be seized with dread and anguish. He confided to them something that shows his humanity: “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch.” He did not hide his pain from his closest friends.

Then he went a little farther, fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.” Notice his way of praying: he is sincere in saying what he feels, but he ends by yielding entirely to the Father's will.

This scene teaches us that praying is not pretending not to be afraid. Jesus says “Abba,” which is an intimate way of saying “Papa.” From within his anguish, he drew near to God as a son who trusts. When our strength runs out, we too can turn to the Father, tell him everything we feel and rest in the fact that his will is good. This is how a hard day ends well: with a surrendered heart.
t.c: Now leave in God's hands what has weighed on you during the day and give thanks that you have made it this far. He knows your weariness and surrounds you with his care. May you sleep in peace tonight, and may his consolation gladden your soul.
m: There are nights when the heart feels heavy. Sometimes we cannot explain why; other times we know, and that is precisely what robs us of sleep. The scene in Gethsemane offers us a very precious teaching: Jesus, the Son of God, also knew anguish, and he did not hide it. He brought it into prayer.

Observe what he did. First, he sought a quiet place. Then he asked his friends to accompany him. Then he spoke with complete sincerity to the Father. And finally, he yielded his desire to the will of God. We can imitate this path. Before sleeping, set aside a corner of quiet, even if it is the edge of the bed. Tell God, without frills, what is worrying you. Then ask that his will be done and that he give you peace to accept it.

The psalmist writes something very close to this experience: “When I thought, ‘My foot slips,’ your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up.” And he adds: “When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul.” God does not promise there will be no moments of worry, but he promises that his consolations will reach our heart if we allow them.

Before closing the day, do something concrete: give thanks in a low voice for three good things that happened today, however small. Then name one burden and consciously hand it over. If needed, repeat a short prayer, such as “Father, I am in your hands.” You have nothing else to settle tonight. The God who sustained Jesus in the garden sustains you too, and his mercy will not let you fall.
